title: Every act an offering
hook: one stretch of sound holds four words, and Arjuna asks why he can't just stop
carry: every act can be an offering to god
tomorrow: Sam wants a Sanskrit tattoo for graduation. good idea?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna dropped his bow, and Krishna answered: your right is to the act, never its fruit. The danda split the line in two. Today, a puzzle in its first stretch, and Arjuna's next question.
screen: `THE ACT IS YOURS, NEVER THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Say did you eat yet, fast, to a friend across a kitchen, and it comes out as one long slur. Sanskrit writes that slur down. The first stretch of Nani's line, karmanyevadhikaraste, sits under one unbroken head line, and inside it are four words: karmani, in action; eva, only; adhikarah, the right; te, yours. Their edges melted as they were said, and the grammarians call that melting sandhi, joining. One stretch of sound you can't pull apart without breaking it. Arjuna is about to learn that a life and its actions are like that too.

In the Gita's third chapter, Arjuna pushes back. If knowing is higher than doing, he asks Krishna, why are you urging me into this terrible act? It's a very human question: if acting gets you tangled, why not step back from all of it? Krishna's answer: you can't. No one can stay even a moment without acting, he says, and even keeping a body alive takes action. Simply not starting work sets no one free. So the real question isn't whether to act. It's how. And here Krishna hands over one of the Gita's great keys. Action binds, he says, except action done as yajna, as an offering. Later he says it to Arjuna plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. That's why, in many Hindu homes, food is set before God before anyone eats, and comes back as prasad, a blessed gift. It's why some people end a task or a meal with a short line: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. The work doesn't change. What it's for changes. Many teachers read this as the other half of yesterday's verse: you let go of the fruit by giving it away before it arrives. Like the words in sandhi, the act and the offering are said in one breath.
screen: `WHY NOT JUST STOP?` · `NO ONE STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `ACTION AS YAJNA, AN OFFERING.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, OFFER IT TO ME.` · `FOOD OFFERED, PRASAD RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary thing you'll do today: a meal, a shift, homework, a call home. Breathe slowly and, if you pray, offer it before you start, in your own words or with the old line, Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. If you don't pray, offer it to someone it will help. Then sit, and let the task feel a little less like yours alone.
Devanagari: a script where one head line can hold several words, joined by sandhi just as they're said.
Pocket this: every act can be an offering to God, the meal, the work, the day. Rest well.

sandhi.meaning: joining: the sound changes where words meet

adhikarah.meaning: the right, in the Gita's line about action

yajna.meaning: sacrifice, offering; action done for God

prasad.meaning: food offered to God and shared as a blessing

Krishnarpanam.meaning: offered to Krishna; said after an act or a meal

notes: Answers 1436's question. Sandhi in 2.47: karmaṇi + eva > karmaṇy eva (i to y before a vowel, Ashtadhyayi 6.1.77); eva + adhikāraḥ > evādhikāraḥ (like vowels to a long vowel, 6.1.101); adhikāraḥ + te > adhikāras te (visarga to s before t, 8.3.34). Confirm the rule numbers.

The hook says 'several words' in the voice; the chat has Priya quoting Nani as 'like four words', which is what the text has (karmaṇi, eva, adhikāraḥ, te). Paraphrase of the clause: 'your right is in action only'.
Gloss 'adhikarah' gives 'uh-dhi-KAH-ruh' (visarga not voiced in the sound-out). 'Panini' gloss says 'ancient' without a date.
